words.technical: Short-term momentum is still strong — the 21-day reading sits at +1.7 standard deviations — but the medium-term components are mixed, with the half-year component negative and the one-year firmly positive. The price sits almost exactly in the middle of its one-year range after the week's fall, and daily volatility near 1.4% remains elevated for this metal. The computed stance is Hold, with the flip level just below the current price, so another Friday like this one would tip it.
words.macro: Gold spent the week in a holding pattern near its highs and then fell over 3% on Friday alone, ending near $4,454, after the new Fed chair used his Jackson Hole debut to warn that inflation is not meaningfully slowing — market-implied odds of a September rate hike roughly doubled on the speech. The setup was already fragile: Wednesday's July PCE print came in at 3.7% year-over-year against 3.6% expected, keeping the pressure on real yields that a hiking turn would amplify.
words.long_term: The structural picture is unchanged: persistent official-sector buying and deteriorating fiscal arithmetic in the large economies keep the long-term backdrop supportive, even through policy-driven air pockets like this one.

eoy_scenarios.central: The September decision passes without a sustained rise in real yields, the debasement worry that powered the August rally neither returns in force nor unwinds, and gold consolidates inside the central band.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Fed backs away from tightening or the fiscal-credibility worry reignites, the dollar's bounce fades, and safe-haven and official-sector demand push gold through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A genuine hiking cycle takes hold, real yields grind higher through the autumn, and the crowded long positioning built during the August rally unwinds through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: The 21-day reading is still positive at +1.2 standard deviations, but the medium-term components are negative and the price now sits in the lower third of its one-year range — a much weaker position than gold's after the same Friday shock. Daily volatility near 2.7% is the highest of the metals, which is why the computed stance steps aside to Flat here, with the flip level several dollars above the market.
words.macro: Silver touched a two-month high above $70 on Thursday, still riding expanded Treasury buybacks of long-dated debt, a persistent physical supply deficit and industrial demand, then fell about 4.5% on Friday to around $66.15 after the hawkish Jackson Hole speech — the entire weekly loss was one session. Monday's own price reporting had the metal up more than 18% month-over-month, a measure of how much froth the speech punctured.
words.long_term: The structural deficit story — industrial demand from electrification and AI-related build-out against constrained mine supply — remains intact and is unaffected by one policy-driven washout.

eoy_scenarios.central: Industrial demand and the supply deficit keep a floor under the metal while the policy shock caps the speculative premium, leaving silver chopping inside the central band.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The debasement trade resumes with gold and the industrial deficit tightens further, restoring the August highs and carrying the price through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hiking Fed and a firm dollar keep squeezing the leveraged length out of the metal, and the unwind carries it through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: The trend components are mildly positive at the half-year and one-year horizons but flat at 21 days, and the price sits near the middle of its one-year range. Daily volatility around 2.8% stays war-elevated. The computed stance remains Flat, with the flip level far above the market near $91.5 — the numbers want persuasion before rejoining this trend.
words.macro: WTI settled Friday at $83.40 and lost more than 4% on the week (Brent more than 5%), as traders read the Iran confrontation as sanctions and economic pressure rather than imminent military supply loss, helped by rumors of an arrangement to keep shipping moving through the Strait of Hormuz — transits stayed erratic, seven vessels one day against seventeen the day before. The counter-current is in products, not crude: Ukrainian strikes overnight Wednesday knocked out the NORSI refinery, Russia's second-largest gasoline producer, leaving all major Lukoil refineries in Russia offline.
words.long_term: The market still carries a structural war-risk premium — Gulf exports are running several million barrels a day below pre-war levels — so the long-term range stays wide and headline-sensitive in both directions.

eoy_scenarios.central: The sanctions-not-war reading holds, Hormuz shipping keeps moving, and crude drifts inside the central band with product markets carrying the war premium instead.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Hormuz arrangement fails or the refinery war escalates into crude infrastructure, and the supply-loss scenario the market just discounted returns above the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: De-escalation extends to a broader settlement, the war premium deflates, and softening demand lets crude sink through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: Bitcoin carries the strongest computed trend on the board — both the 21-day and quarter readings sit above +1.5 standard deviations — while the price is parked almost exactly mid-range for the year. Daily volatility near 2.5% is ordinary for the asset. The stance stays Hold, and the flip level near $74,000 leaves room for a normal pullback before anything changes.
words.macro: The coin spent Friday pinned around $80,000, just under its $83,000 August peak, with the whole market treating the new Fed chair's 10:00 ET Jackson Hole debut as the binary event of the week — and the hawkish outcome, which roughly doubled September rate-hike pricing, pushed it back under $78,000 into the weekend. A week that closes down less than 1% therefore hides a sharp Friday reversal, the same pattern as the metals.
words.long_term: The structural picture is unchanged: institutional adoption and the debasement narrative support the asset across quarters, while its correlation with policy-sensitive risk assets keeps every Fed inflection a two-way event.

eoy_scenarios.central: Policy settles after September, the August peak caps the market for a while, and bitcoin works sideways inside the central band with the trend intact.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Fed stands down and the debasement trade resumes, carrying the coin through its August high and above the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hiking cycle drains risk appetite, the mid-range support gives way, and the retreat extends through the bottom of the band.

words.technical: The index sits in the upper fifth of its one-year range with every trend horizon positive except the quarter, and short-term momentum near +0.9 standard deviations. Daily volatility around 1.2% is roughly double the broad market's. The stance is Hold with the flip level about 2.5% below the market — an ordinary shakeout would not reach it.
words.macro: The week was two opposite sessions: Thursday the index rose 1.4% on a very narrow rally — Nvidia added 8.7% and about $442 billion of market value after guiding to roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, with Salesforce and CrowdStrike up over 20% on their own results — while the equal-weight broad market actually fell. Friday the hawkish Jackson Hole debut took back half of it, and the index still closed the week modestly higher; the concentration, not the direction, is the story.
words.long_term: The AI capital-spending cycle keeps earnings momentum in a handful of mega-caps; the index's long-term path is increasingly the path of that spending, for better and for worse.

eoy_scenarios.central: AI earnings keep delivering while the Fed stays merely watchful, and the index grinds inside the central band on narrow leadership.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The spending cycle broadens beyond the mega-caps and policy stays benign, extending the rally through the top of the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: A hiking Fed compresses multiples exactly where the crowding is worst, and the narrow leadership that lifted the index takes it below the band on the way out.

words.technical: The 21-day reading is slightly negative but the medium horizons are positive, and the index sits in the upper part of its one-year range after the Friday jump. Daily volatility near 0.3% is, as always, the lowest on the board. The computed stance is Flat with the flip level at 100.17 — the week's close is within half a per cent of flipping it to Hold.
words.macro: The dollar index rose 0.59% on Friday to 99.69 — its biggest one-day gain since mid-June — and about 0.9% on the week, its best in ten weeks, after the new Fed chair said the Fed "will have work to do" if inflation does not cool; September hike pricing jumped from roughly a third to well over half. Wednesday's hotter-than-expected July PCE print had already set the direction, and the ECB's own September 10 decision now frames the euro side of the pair.
words.long_term: The long-term picture remains a tug-of-war between rate differentials, which the week moved in the dollar's favour, and the fiscal-credibility worry that drove the summer's debasement trade against it.

eoy_scenarios.central: Rate differentials and fiscal worry roughly offset, and the index oscillates in its narrow central band through year-end.
eoy_scenarios.upside: The Fed actually hikes while the ECB holds, and the differential carries the index above the band.
eoy_scenarios.downside: The hawkish repricing unwinds or the debt worry returns to the front page, and the index slides back through the bottom of the band.

week_summary: The week belonged to the new Fed chair's Jackson Hole debut: a hawkish first speech on Friday flipped September pricing from a hold toward a possible hike, handed the dollar its best week in ten, knocked gold and silver off multi-month highs and pushed bitcoin back under $78,000 — while a narrow, Nvidia-led tech rally still left the big US indices slightly higher on the week, and oil lost more than 4% as traders read the Iran confrontation as sanctions pressure rather than imminent supply loss.
